description: Granular reload via the path_filter input on system.control.reload_module. path_filter and module_id are mutually exclusive (MODULE_RELOAD_CONFLICT). A path_filter matching zero modules is a no-op. Reload order MUST follow dependency topological order. PROTOCOL_SPEC 6.7 clause 4 fixes the matcher: path_filter is a GLOB-DIALECT pattern matched with algorithm A25 (9.2.3) against each registered module ID — `*` and `?` only, every other character literal, and NO pattern is ever rejected. Until v1.37.0 this clause said only 'glob' and the three SDKs used three matchers (fnmatch, A08, the glob crate), so one control-plane request reloaded two modules, reloaded none, or was refused as malformed depending on which SDK served it. Every case below except the first uses a value from outside the trailing-star family, which is the only family the three agreed on. See docs/features/system-modules.md#14-granular-reload-via-path-filtering.

expected._note: Only matching IDs are re-discovered and reloaded.
Existing module_id-based single reload is unchanged when path_filter is absent.
Zero matches MUST NOT raise; reloaded_modules is empty.
Providing both module_id and path_filter MUST raise MODULE_RELOAD_CONFLICT.

test_cases._why: DISCRIMINATING — apcore-typescript matches path_filter with A08, where `?` is a LITERAL, so this reloads nothing while Python (fnmatch) and Rust (glob) reload two modules. reload_path_filter's own rule that a zero-match filter is a silent no-op is what makes the divergence invisible: TypeScript returns success with an empty list.

DISCRIMINATING — `glob::Pattern::new("a[b")` is an ERROR in apcore-rust ('invalid range pattern'), so the request FAILS there while the other two serve it. Under A25 every string is a valid pattern (9.2.3 requirement 2): `a[b` is a literal name, matches no registered module, and the call is an ordinary no-op.

DISCRIMINATING — apcore-python (fnmatch) and apcore-rust (glob) both expand `[em]` as a character class and reload four modules. A25 has no classes, so the pattern names a literal segment that no module carries and the call is a no-op.

DISCRIMINATING — `glob::Pattern::new("executor.email.**")` is an ERROR in apcore-rust ('recursive wildcards must form a single path component'). Under A25 the empty interior segment is a no-op, so this behaves exactly like a single trailing star.

test_cases.description:
D-121: `reload_dependents` is DEPRECATED and ignored. Declared in all three SDKs' input schemas and read by none — a spec MUST that no implementation satisfied, which is the §9.1.3 'declared surface reaches no mechanism' shape applied to a module input field. Three independent implementations skipping it is the evidence the maintainer decision rests on: deprecate now, remove at 2.0, do NOT implement.

The reloaded set is asserted IDENTICAL to `glob_filter_restricts_rediscovery`, which runs the same filter without the field. Asserting only that the call succeeds would pass for an SDK that started honouring it and pulled the dependents in.

The once-per-instance deprecation WARNING is pinned by per-SDK tests instead: it is instance state, and a fixture case cannot observe it without depending on which case ran first in the process.

AT 2.0 THIS CASE FLIPS rather than being deleted: the field is removed, the input schema sets `additionalProperties: false`, and the same input becomes a validation error.

D-111: a bulk reload writes one audit entry PER MODULE, and every entry from that one reload carries the SAME correlation id.

apcore-python and apcore-rust wrote a single aggregate entry whose `target_module_id` was the glob. `AuditStore.query(module_id)` filters on a concrete id, so that entry is unfindable by the accessor the store exists for — the operation was audited and could not be looked up. Asserting the entry COUNT alone would pass for an aggregate entry if the glob happened to match one module, which is why the expected targets are listed explicitly.

The correlation id is asserted as a property (all equal, non-empty) rather than as a value: it is generated per call. Per-module entries alone lose the fact that they were one deploy, so a fresh id per entry groups nothing — and a constant groups every deploy together, which is pinned by per-SDK tests running two reloads.
